title: AppBench: Benchmarking AI-Generated Web Applications
authors: Ethan Hellman, Brendan McLaughlin, Abhinav Lalwani, Belinda Mo
problem: Code benchmarks check functions with unit tests. Nothing checked whether an AI-built web app is usable: does navigation work, does state survive a refresh, are errors handled?
method: 9 app requests from L0 (static page) to L4 (real-time collaborative whiteboard), spread over six axes (UI, features, state, API integration, cross-page navigation, data processing). Each request gets a checklist of explicit and implicit requirements, arranged as a dependency graph and turned into a scripted evaluator built from shared tools: screenshot + multimodal LLM judging, an LLM-driven browser (Stagehand on Playwright), and network interception for error states. Weighted scores scaled to 0-100. 7 builders tested one-shot: Replit, Bolt, Cursor Agent, Lovable, Claude Sonnet 3.7, GPT-4.5, OpenHands CodeAct 2.1.
results: Grader vs. 3 human raters: mean MSE 0.0302, mean MAE 0.1313, Pearson 0.8173, Spearman 0.6827. Per-builder MSE from 0.0160 (Service 4) to 0.0501 (CodeAct); per-task MSE from 0.0042 (l2-add-to-cart) to 0.0751 (l3-food-order). All builder types scored above 75% up to L2, fell at L3 and dropped sharply at L4; 2 of 7 builders failed to produce a compiling app for one L3 and one L4 task. One-shot models were close to full agent products; Lovable and Bolt were the top builders.
lessons: Grade AI-built software by what a user can do with it, not by whether it compiles. Split checks into what was asked and what a good result would also do, and skip checks whose prerequisites failed so one root failure doesn't look like ten. Validate your grader against humans (or at least known-good and known-broken examples) before trusting it. Don't assume an agent framework beats a strong one-shot model; measure it.
rebuild: The local model builds 5 single-file HTML apps (L0-L3: about page, theme switcher, tip calculator, food order, to-do list saved in localStorage). Python's HTML parser checks structure; Node.js runs each app's script in a fake page (subprocess with timeout) and calls the functions it exposes on window.app, including a 'page refresh' test for saved state. Checks are weighted, core vs. implicit, with dependencies. We validate the grader on known-good/broken apps, compare one-shot vs. one fix round with failure feedback, and (in the solutions) correlate the grader with a hand score and an LLM judge.

title: PRIME: Planning with Reflective Iterative Multi-Agentic Exploration
authors: Chelsea Zou, Samuel Liu, Jui Khankari (the poster lists Chelsea Zou, Jui Khankari, Miriam Cheng)
problem: Reasoning tricks such as reflection, debate and voting are applied ad hoc, with no principled way to choose the right one for each step of a multi-step plan.
method: Treat each reasoning technique as an 'option' and search with Monte Carlo Tree Search. A planner splits the task into subgoals; at each node it can Drill down, Solve with the best-suited self-improvement tool (self-reflection, self-refinement, debate), or Backtrack. Values are backed up with a running mean and nodes chosen with UCT; non-leaf values mix an LM score with self-consistency. Built on LATS. GPT-4o-mini inside PRIME, compared with LATS, plain 4o-mini and one-shot o1 on 60 sampled questions each from PlanBench, WebShop and Game of 24, plus a reverse ablation that upgrades only the planner or only the executor.
results: Table 1 success rates (PlanBench / WebShop / Game of 24): PRIME 36.2% / 40% / 75%; LATS 2.2% / 38% / 44%; GPT-4o-mini 0% / 0% / 0%; GPT-o1 100% / 100% / 100%; PRIME with upgraded planner 95% / 94% / 100%; with upgraded executor 96% / 92% / 100%. The text gives different figures for some cells (PRIME 'a 2.2% improvement over LATS' on PlanBench; o1 at 37.3% on PlanBench and 80% on WebShop), so these numbers are internally inconsistent. Estimated about 4x lower cost than o1 despite more API calls.
lessons: Choosing the strategy per subgoal can beat one fixed strategy, but compare at equal call budgets: on WebShop, PRIME and LATS tied and reflections were generic. Tree search shines when each step's result is clear and checkable, and wanders when it isn't. A reverse ablation (upgrade one component at a time) is a cheap way to find which part of a pipeline deserves the expensive model.
rebuild: Game of 24 with an exact ast-based checker. PRIME-lite: the planner proposes first steps with a confidence (LM value); code drops impossible steps (backtrack); a bandit-style MCTS picks (subgoal, tool) arms with UCT across three tools (solve, reflect, drill down), uses the checker as reward, backs up values with the paper's running mean, and carries tool statistics across puzzles. Compared at a 5-call budget against single-shot and retry-with-feedback; solutions run a reverse ablation with a 3B executor and vary the exploration constant.

title: Enhancing Mathematical Reasoning in LLMs through Reasoning Distillation, GRPO, and Multi-agent PRM Reranking
authors: Abhinav Agarwal, Shree Reddy, Carlo Baronio, Shubhra Mishra
problem: Olympiad-level math (the AIMO prize) needs long, consistent reasoning, and models spend many tokens getting there.
method: A 387K-problem dataset (OpenR1-Math-220K 55%, 150K newly generated 37.5%, Bespoke-Stratos-17K 7.5%; a GPT-4o-mini judge rejected about 15% of generated solutions). Chain-of-thought distillation from DeepSeek R1 into Qwen2.5 with a KL + cross-entropy loss and a falling temperature. GRPO with KL penalty beta = 0 (no reference model), reward 1.0 for correctness + 0.2 for format, DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 and colocated vLLM, scaled to 32B. At test time, several solvers, self-verification, and a (preference) reward model reranks candidates.
results: AIME'24: 32B GRPO model 76.7% with 5,048 tokens per problem vs. 32K for baselines (reported as a 6.3x reduction); 79.9% with multi-agent reranking over 4 passes. Ablation: base 50.0%, distillation only 72.1% (+22.1), + GRPO 76.7% (+4.6), + reranking 79.9% (+3.2). Baselines: Qwen2.5-32B Instruct 26.7%, Qwen2.5-Math-72B 30.0% (40.0% with tool-integrated reasoning), R1-Distill-Qwen-32B 73.3%. Qwen2.5-1.5B GRPO 10.0%, 7B GRPO 16.7%; their 7B pipeline 65.2% (5,137 tokens) vs. 58.7% baseline. 2.1x faster inference. Context window had to grow from 8,192 to 16,384 tokens after about 320 GRPO steps on 7B. Reward-model selection beat majority voting at every size (e.g., Qwen2.5-Math-7B 70.0% rm@64 vs. 43.3% maj@64). Note: AIME'24 has 30 problems, and 79.9% is not a multiple of 1/30; the paper does not explain this.
lessons: Most of the gain came from distillation (good data from a stronger model), not RL; RL then mostly bought token efficiency. Filter distillation data with a checker, including the steps, not just the final answer. A verifier that scores candidates beats majority voting when the right answer is rare. Setting the KL penalty to 0 saves a whole model's memory and worked here. Watch for truncated completions during RL.
rebuild: Seeded word problems from lal.tasks. Distillation data: llama3.1:8b samples 2 rationales per problem; we keep only those with the right answer and no wrong calculation, and choose the shortest, writing a ready-to-train SFT JSONL. Reranking: llama3.2:3b writes 4 solutions per test problem; we compare first sample, majority vote, a code step-checker used as a process reward (min over steps), an LLM judge that names the first wrong step, and the pass@4 oracle. Behind RUN_LONG: GRPO with TRL on SmolLM2-135M-Instruct using the paper's 1.0 + 0.2 reward and beta = 0 (fp32 on T4), and SFT on the distilled file.

title: Towards Effective Meta-Agents: Designing Agents that Design Agents (paper: Inefficiencies of Meta Agents for Agent Design)
authors: Batu El, Mert Yuksekgonul, James Zou
problem: Meta-agents such as ADAS write new agents in a sample-evaluate-iterate loop. Do they learn from past designs, are the designs diverse enough to combine, and is the design cost ever worth it?
method: Archive starts with 7 hand-written agents (Chain-of-Thought, Majority Voting, Refinement from Feedback, LLM Debate, Quality-Diversity, Routing, Step-back). A gpt-4o meta-agent writes agent code run on gpt-3.5, for 30 iterations, with three context strategies: cumulative (all past agents, as in ADAS), parallel (only the initial library), evolutionary (top 7 so far). MGSM, DROP, MMLU (128 train / 200 test) and GPQA (32 / 160), 3 runs. Diversity via cosine similarity of per-question score vectors and coverage; economics via total cost C0 + n*Cj.
results: Best agent's train score, averaged over datasets: cumulative 55.0, parallel 60.0, evolutionary 60.3 (cumulative did not beat parallel). Evolutionary up to +10 points over cumulative on MGSM (41.4 vs. 56.5 train). Test score of the best-on-train agent, average: initial library 49.0, cumulative 52.2, parallel 55.9, evolutionary 55.2. Coverage average: cumulative 94.2%, parallel 95.9%, evolutionary 94.4%; evolutionary agents were the least diverse. Designed agents cost more per query than the initial ones (cumulative > evolutionary > parallel > initial). The designed agent becomes cheaper per correct answer only after about 15,000 queries, and only on MMLU and DROP with parallel context; elsewhere never.
lessons: Before building a self-improving agent designer, do the cost arithmetic: design cost plus higher per-query cost often never pays back. Showing the meta-agent everything it has tried can be worse than showing nothing; curate the context (best parents). Designed agents tend to be similar, so 'pick the best per query' gains are limited unless you push for diversity. Meta-evaluation is noisy; use several runs.
rebuild: Six kinds of checkable puzzles (letter counts, reversing, sorting, weekdays, word problems, decimal comparison). Designs are data (system prompt + one of four fixed procedures), so no model-written code runs. llama3.1:8b is the meta-agent, llama3.2:3b runs agents. Starting library of 3, evolutionary context for 3 iterations, archive with score vectors, train/test comparison, cosine similarity and coverage, a break-even calculation with C0 + n*Cj, and in the solutions a parallel-context run (RUN_LONG), a per-kind router and a pricing what-if.

title: ARCHON Augmented: Planning and Web-Enhanced Components
authors: Megan Mou, Sherry Xie, Emily Zhang, Andrew Park
problem: Archon stacks inference-time techniques (generate, fuse, critique, rank, verify, unit tests) but has only seven building blocks, no tool use or web search, and its strong results relied on about 70B models.
method: Three new blocks: a Planner at the front (rephrase + step-by-step plan passed to later blocks), an Expander after each generator (adds context so critics and rankers can judge), and a Web Search Tool Call (queries from the plan, top 10 Google results per query). Ablations on a closed-source configuration (GPT-4o generate/rank, Qwen2-72B critic/fuser) and an open-source ensemble, on a 500-question subset of Humanity's Last Exam (453 scored) and AlpacaEval (length-controlled win rate).
results: HLE (closed / open): ARCHON 3.3% / 3.3%; + Planner 3.3% / 2.6%; + Planner + Expander 4.2% (19/453) / 3.8% (17/453); + Planner + Tool Call + Expander 3.3% / 2.9%. Zero-shot GPT-4o 3.1%. AlpacaEval LC (closed / mixed): ARCHON 67.73% / 57.01%; + Planner 69.62% / 67.06%; + Planner + Expander 66.01% / 68.30%; + Planner + Tool Call + Expander 73.40% / 73.92%. Web search hurt on HLE because results were off-topic or cluttered.
lessons: A planner at the front of a pipeline is cheap and helped weaker open models catch up on instruction following. Search helps only if retrieval is precise; noisy pages can make answers worse. The value of each block depends on the task, so ablate each one on your own data. Small differences on a hard benchmark (a few questions out of 453) are noise.
rebuild: Questions about made-up towns (so search is required) over 16 local 'web pages', including look-alike decoy pages and clutter, searched with a 15-line BM25. Compares a single call, single call + search (RAG), planner + search + 1 generator, and the full pipeline: planner (plan + queries) -> BM25 search -> 3 generators (8B, 8B, 3B) -> critic + ranker -> fuser -> verifier with fallback. Reports accuracy and calls per question; solutions ablate the fuser/verifier for free, score each generator, and test a noisier web.
